stem.en: A car moves at 20 m/s. The driver speeds up to 40 m/s, and later brakes until the car stops. What happens to the car's kinetic energy?

text.en: It becomes four times as large, then falls to zero.
It becomes twice as large, then falls to zero.
It becomes four times as large, then turns negative.
It becomes twice as large, then stays the same.

explanation.en: Doubling the speed makes the kinetic energy four times as large, because the speed is squared in K = 1/2 mv^2. Braking does negative work, so the kinetic energy falls. It reaches zero when the car stops. Kinetic energy can never be negative, because mass and v^2 are never negative.

hints.en: What happens to v^2 when v doubles?
Can kinetic energy be less than zero?
